en: Nairātmyasiddhi:
Homage to the Buddha!
That which has no connection whatsoever with another does not possess that [other].

For example, there is no connection whatsoever between the Himalaya and the Malaya mountains, which are stable by nature, [just as there is none] with the living body; this is the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). This reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*), because if a connection were to exist, it would have to be either identity (*tādātmya*) or origination from that (*tadutpatti*).
Nor is there identity between the self and the body,
because the body possesses such characteristics as impermanence,
whereas the self is accepted as being the opposite of that.
Nor can it be arising from that [the body], because the production of a body is impossible for an eternal self,
nor can an eternal self arise from a body.
If it is argued that the relationship between those two is characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*),
then what is the relationship between those two and that [conjunction] itself?
If it is argued that it is inherence (*samavāya*), then...
Furthermore, what relation do they have with that [inherence]?
If another relation is admitted, there is an infinite regress; if it is not admitted, then inherence does not belong to them.
Likewise, even if one were to postulate another relationship between the self and the body, this very same example would apply; thus, there is no lack of proof (asiddhi) for this reason,
nor is it contradictory (viruddha), because it exists in the similar class (sapakṣa).
Nor is inconclusiveness observed,
because the conventional usage of "possessing that" is pervaded by its being based on a relation,
since it would follow that even in the absence of a relation, such usage would lack a restricted object; thus it is established.
The proof of selflessness (*nairātmyasiddhi*) is completed, even by way of [the reason's] being inconclusive (*anaikāntikatā*). Manuscript notes: *naimittika* and *nairātmyasiddhiḥ samāptā*.
